title: What is the ILO, and why does it matter to Indian workers?
author: Editorial Desk
summary: A short guide to the International Labour Organization and its unusual three-party structure.
body:
The **International Labour Organization (ILO)** is the United Nations agency for the world of work. It was created in **1919**, and India has been a member from the start. Its headquarters are in Geneva, Switzerland.

## Tripartite by design

What makes the ILO different from other UN agencies is that it is **tripartite**. Each member country sends a delegation with representatives of the government, of employers and of workers. Workers' representatives are chosen from the most representative trade union centres of that country. This is why the voice of an organisation like BMS is heard at Geneva.

## What it does

- Sets **international labour standards**, called Conventions and Recommendations, on subjects such as forced labour, child labour, equal remuneration, non-discrimination, safety at work and freedom of association.
- Provides **technical assistance** to governments and social partners.
- Collects and publishes **research and statistics** on employment and decent work.

## The annual conference

Once a year, in June, member countries meet in Geneva for the **International Labour Conference (ILC)**. The conference adopts standards, discusses reports and holds a plenary at which leaders of delegations speak. BMS has regularly sent delegations to the ILC and its leaders have addressed the plenary on behalf of the workers of India.

## Why it matters at home

Many Indian labour laws, from minimum wages to prohibition of child labour, are influenced by ILO standards. And when the Government of India, trade unions and employers sit together at Geneva, they negotiate positions that affect every worker back home.

The next posts in this series will follow BMS delegations to Geneva, year by year.
